clue.text: Makes a bequest or an easy conquest

definitions.meaning: to pass something on to heirs is to give it down the generations
to win by a wide margin, without effort, is an idiomatic victory

explanation.definitionFit: A double definition: the phrasal verb means passing property to heirs, and the idiom means winning with ease.

clue.text: Latter part of 14 is, perhaps, an archbishop

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the letters may be arranged otherwise

parts.note: 14-across is CAPITAL CHARGE, whose second word is charge

explanation.surface: A remark on a bishop's title, as though following some numbered item.
explanation.definitionFit: An archbishop is formally addressed as His Grace, an honorific form of address.

clue.text: Rover giving assent to receive a degree

indicators.note: to receive means one piece takes another inside it

parts.note: a nod gives agreement
an MA is a Master of Arts degree

explanation.surface: A wanderer agrees to accept a university qualification.
explanation.definitionFit: A nomad roams from place to place, so is a rover.

clue.text: Solar gravity?

parts.note: the pull of our nearest star read literally, as well as the draw of a celebrity performer

explanation.definitionFit: A big-name performer draws crowds, just as a star's gravity draws in bodies.

clue.text: Course not much spoken about, like the M25

indicators.note: about means one word goes around the other

parts.note: oral means spoken
a bit is a small amount

explanation.surface: A route seldom discussed, compared with London's ring motorway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Course' sits with the definition: an orbital is a ring road, and the M25 is the motorway that circles London.
explanation.definitionFit: The M25 encircles London, so it is described as an orbital motorway, one going round.

clue.text: Electronic payment discounted?

definitions.meaning: money sent over the internet, the net
net money is what remains after deductions

explanation.definitionFit: A double definition: internet money, and a sum left after deductions, the net amount.

clue.text: Comply with unknown order

parts.note: the OBE is the Order of the British Empire, a British honour
algebra's unknowns are x, y and z; here Y

explanation.surface: An instruction to go along with some unexplained command.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unknown order' reads as one mysterious command, but it splits into an unknown (Y) and an order (OBE), set down in answer order.
explanation.definitionFit: To do as you are told is to comply with a rule or instruction, a plain synonym.

clue.text: Drinks laced with spirit — no start for those unaccustomed

indicators.note: drinks laced with spirit have spirit put into them

parts.note: beers are drinks
gin is a spirit

indicators.note: start means only the opening letter of the word is used

explanation.surface: Spiked beers are no way to start for those not used to alcohol.
explanation.definitionFit: Beginners are novices, people not yet used to something.

clue.text: Treaty formulation requires a lot of talk

indicators.note: formulation means the letters are formed into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Drafting an international agreement involves endless discussion.
explanation.definitionFit: Yatter is informal for incessant chatter, a lot of idle talk.

clue.text: It may or may not deserve to be opened at customs

definitions.text: It may or may not deserve to be opened at customs

parts.words: It may or may not deserve to be opened at customs
parts.note: a suitcase at a frontier which might or might not merit inspection

explanation.definitionFit: A doubtful case, either way; here literally a case at a border.

clue.text: Boy with degree in 13, but not first class

parts.note: Sam is a boy's name
a BA is a Bachelor of Arts degree

explanation.surface: A young man with a qualification is somehow inside some second-rate item.
explanation.walkthrough: 13 is AIDANCE; 'not first class' takes away AI (A1, first class), leaving DANCE. 'In' links the definition: a samba is in the class of dances.
explanation.definitionFit: The samba is a Brazilian ballroom form, an example of a dance.

clue.text: Girl should have considered

parts.note: Beth is a girl's name
'ought' expresses obligation, what one should do

explanation.surface: A young woman ought to have thought it over.
explanation.definitionFit: To bethink oneself is an old word for reflect, so its past tense is a synonym for considered.

clue.text: The Guardian rehashed with huge bits removed could look like the Sun

indicators.note: rehashed means the remaining letters are reworked into a new order

parts.note: the four letters of this word are the ones taken away

explanation.surface: Someone remakes this newspaper and cuts out the big stories, making it resemble a tabloid rival.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With huge bits removed' tells you to take H, U, G and E out of THE GUARDIAN, leaving TARDIAN, which 'rehashed' rearranges. The Sun is also a British tabloid newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: Something radiant shines brightly, as the sun in the sky does.

clue.text: Help given to church by a saint

parts.note: St Aidan was a seventh-century missionary saint in Northumbria
CE stands for the Church of England

explanation.surface: Assistance offered to a church by a holy man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Given to' and 'by' are link words joining the saint to the church; the surface's donor saint is really just a name.
explanation.definitionFit: Aidance is an old word for assistance or support, a synonym of help.

clue.text: Ken's road tax might be treason

definitions.meaning: Ken Livingstone, as Mayor of London, introduced the congestion charge, a fee for driving in the capital
treason was a crime punishable by death, a hanging offence

explanation.definitionFit: A double definition: a fee levied in the capital city, and an accusation carrying the death penalty.

clue.text: Propositions for where they say one can't smoke

indicators.note: they say means the word is spoken, giving a word with the same sound

parts.note: notices say smoking is not allowed on these premises, a building and its grounds

explanation.surface: Ideas offered about places where smoking is banned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Where' links to the no-smoking sign. Premisses, with double S, is a spelling of the logician's term.
explanation.definitionFit: In logic a premiss is a statement assumed as the basis of an argument, so the plural are propositions.

clue.text: Drink spilt over tray! One can't be trusted

indicators.note: a drink spilt over a tray surrounds it

parts.note: beer is a drink

explanation.surface: Someone spills beer on a tray and is declared unreliable.
explanation.definitionFit: A betrayer is a traitor, someone not to be trusted.

clue.text: Take the pill?

parts.note: taking the contraceptive pill avoids offspring, read here as dodging a matter under discussion

explanation.definitionFit: To avoid a question or topic, with issue's second sense of children giving the joke.

clue.text: Before Warwick, say — that's the last kingmaker

parts.note: the Earl of Warwick is an example of an earl
i.e. stands for 'that is'

indicators.note: last means the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A history note about Warwick the Kingmaker, the last of his kind.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard Neville, Earl of Warwick, was called the Kingmaker in the Wars of the Roses, which makes 'last kingmaker' look like history.
explanation.definitionFit: Earlier means at a previous time, so before.

clue.text: Neck with abandon in the hay — in London?

indicators.note: with abandon means the letters are thrown about wildly

explanation.surface: A couple kissing wildly in a haystack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With abandon' rearranges NECK and HAY; 'in the' is a link. HACKNEY is a borough of East London.
explanation.definitionFit: Hackney is a district of London, an example of a place there.

clue.text: Odd pieces of 5 (part 2)

indicators.note: odd means strange, so the letters appear in a strange order

explanation.surface: A remark on strange coins making up a second instalment.
explanation.walkthrough: 5 is NETCASH; its second part is CASH, which specie means.
explanation.definitionFit: Specie is money in coin, a synonym of hard cash.

clue.text: Single parent could be an artist

indicators.note: could be says these letters may form something else when rearranged

parts.note: one, written as the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A lone mother or father might turn out to be creative.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Could be' rearranges I and PARENT together.
explanation.definitionFit: A painter is one kind of artist, working in paint.

clue.text: City street in comfort

indicators.note: in means the street goes inside the other word

parts.note: to comfort someone is to cheer them

explanation.surface: A city road offering consolation.
explanation.walkthrough: CHESTER is a cathedral city in north-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Chester is an English city in Cheshire, an example of a city.

clue.text: Mean to get drunk

definitions.meaning: intoxicated, slang for having had too much

explanation.definitionFit: A double definition: stingy with money, and slang for intoxicated.

clue.text: Jailer erected studio in prison

indicators.note: in places the rebuilt word inside the slang for jail

parts.note: the can is slang for prison

indicators.note: erected means built, so the letters are constructed into a new form

explanation.surface: A warder put up an artist's workroom in a jail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Erected' means built, an anagram signal; it might suggest reading upwards in a down clue, but a plain reversal of the studio does not fit.
explanation.definitionFit: A custodian is a keeper or guardian, and one who keeps prisoners is a jailer.

clue.text: A useless transport system going spare

parts.note: NG is short for no good
RY is an abbreviation of railway

explanation.surface: A complaint about a hopeless rail network making someone furious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going spare' is British slang for becoming very annoyed.
explanation.definitionFit: To go spare in British slang is to become furious, so the phrase stands for cross.

clue.text: Riser not starting where the sun does

indicators.note: not starting means the first letter is dropped

parts.note: yeast makes dough rise, so it is a riser

explanation.surface: Someone getting up late, rather than at dawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Riser' looks like an early riser, but it is the raising agent; 'the sun does' continues 'riser': where the sun rises.
explanation.definitionFit: The sun rises in this compass direction each morning.

clue.text: Merry's the work of McGonagall, say

indicators.note: work means the letters are worked into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A jolly line said to be by a famously bad poet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Work' rearranges the letters of MERRYS THE; 'of' joins. William McGonagall was a Victorian Scottish versifier famous as the worst poet in English.
explanation.definitionFit: McGonagall wrote doggerel, so he is an example of a writer of crude verse.
